Josquin des Prez. A Franco-Flemish master who lived around 1450 to 1521 and defined the High Renaissance ideal of balanced, emotionally engaging polyphony. His reputation was towering even during his lifetime, and later musicians revered him as the father of musicians.

Josquin composed the motet Ave Maria, Gratia plena, which exemplifies his gift for singable, soaring counterpoint and textual clarity within complex voicing. His revolutionary use of imitative counterpoint meant that each melodic idea would enter in succession across all voices, creating unity and momentum while maintaining independence. He traveled extensively, serving at the courts of Milan, Rome, the Medici, and the House of Burgundy, absorbing local styles and becoming a bridge between national musical traditions.

His masses include the Missa Pange Lingua and Missa Ave Maris Stella, both using cantus firmus technique with extraordinary structural coherence. He was known for text-painting: musical gestures that reflect the meaning of the lyrics. Ascending lines for words like ascended, dissonant clusters for suffering. Such details show his attention to how music and language could work together. The term musica reservata, sometimes attributed to him, captures his philosophy: the idea that music should be performed by skilled singers for discerning audiences, not every crowd. He elevated the cyclic mass to supreme formal achievement and made imitative polyphony in the motet the Renaissance gold standard.
